c01.display: Next stop: Attention Junction! Passport out. Stamped.
c01.spoken: Next stop: Attention Junction! Passport out. Stamped.

c02.display: This is stop number 5 of seven. In Vector Valley, every word got its own place on a map of meaning. Today, the words start talking to each other.
c02.spoken: This is stop number 5 of seven. In Vector Valley, every word got its own place on a map of meaning. Today, the words start talking to each other.

c03.display: Here's a puzzle. The word bank can mean the side of a river, or a place that keeps your money.
c03.spoken: Here's a puzzle. The word bank can mean the side of a river, or a place that keeps your money.

c04.display: On its own, the word can't tell you which. The words around it decide.
c04.spoken: On its own, the word can't tell you which. The words around it decide.

c05.display: On the route map, we've left Vector Valley, and we're here, at Attention Junction, where the model reads the whole sentence together.
c05.spoken: On the route map, we've left Vector Valley, and we're here, at Attention Junction, where the model reads the whole sentence together.

c06.display: At the end of our last stop, we asked: in "the bank of the river", how does the model know which bank you mean? Let's watch.
c06.spoken: At the end of our last stop, we asked: in "the bank of the river", how does the model know which bank you mean? Let's watch.

c07.display: In "I sat on the bank of the river", the word bank looks around the sentence, and looks hardest at river. So this is the riverside.
c07.spoken: In "I sat on the bank of the river", the word bank looks around the sentence, and looks hardest at river. So this is the riverside.

c08.display: Now: "I paid cash into the bank". This time, bank looks at cash and paid. So this is the money kind.
c08.spoken: Now: "I paid cash into the bank". This time, bank looks at cash and paid. So this is the money kind.

c09.display: Same word, same starting vector, but a different meaning, because of what it paid attention to. The percentages on screen are just for illustration, but the idea is real.
c09.spoken: Same word, same starting vector, but a different meaning, because of what it paid attention to. The percentages on screen are just for illustration, but the idea is real.

c10.display: This trick is called attention. Each word looks at every other word in the prompt, decides how much each one matters to it, and blends in a little of their meaning.
c10.spoken: This trick is called attention. Each word looks at every other word in the prompt, decides how much each one matters to it, and blends in a little of their meaning.

c11.display: So bank, plus a lot of river, becomes riverbank.
c11.spoken: So bank, plus a lot of river, becomes riverbank.

c12.display: Think of a busy railway junction. Announcements fill the air, but every traveller only listens for the ones that matter to their own train.
c12.spoken: Think of a busy railway junction. Announcements fill the air, but every traveller only listens for the ones that matter to their own train.

c13.display: Let's try it on our running prompt: "Write a short poem about the rain". What does the word poem pay attention to?
c13.spoken: Let's try it on our running prompt: "Write a short poem about the rain". What does the word poem pay attention to?

c14.display: What kind of poem? A short one. About what? The rain. And write tells it this is a task, not a question.
c14.spoken: What kind of poem? A short one. About what? The rain. And write tells it this is a task, not a question.

c15.display: After attention, poem is no longer just any poem. It now carries the idea of a short poem, about rain, that you want written.
c15.spoken: After attention, poem is no longer just any poem. It now carries the idea of a short poem, about rain, that you want written.

c16.display: Pause and predict. "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." What does it refer to? The animal, the street, or the crossing?
c16.spoken: Pause and predict. "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." What does it refer to? The animal, the street, or the crossing?

c17.display: The answer is the animal. Streets don't get tired. Animals do.
c17.spoken: The answer is the animal. Streets don't get tired. Animals do.

c18.display: Watch the word it. With tired at the end, it looks mostly at animal.
c18.spoken: Watch the word it. With tired at the end, it looks mostly at animal.

c19.display: Now change just one word: "because it was too wide". Suddenly, it looks at street instead. Animals aren't wide. Streets are.
c19.spoken: Now change just one word: "because it was too wide". Suddenly, it looks at street instead. Animals aren't wide. Streets are.

c20.display: One word at the end of the sentence changed how a word in the middle was understood. That's attention working across the whole sentence at once.
c20.spoken: One word at the end of the sentence changed how a word in the middle was understood. That's attention working across the whole sentence at once.

c21.display: So how does a word decide where to look? Here's the idea in four small steps, with no formulas.
c21.spoken: So how does a word decide where to look? Here's the idea in four small steps, with no formulas.

c22.display: First, ask. Every word makes a query: a little description of what it's looking for. The word it is looking for a thing that can be tired.
c22.spoken: First, ask. Every word makes a query: a little description of what it's looking for. The word it is looking for a thing that can be tired.

c23.display: Second, match. Every word also has a key, like a label saying what it offers. The query is compared with every key.
c23.spoken: Second, match. Every word also has a key, like a label saying what it offers. The query is compared with every key.

c24.display: Third, weigh. The match scores are turned into percentages that add up to one hundred.
c24.spoken: Third, weigh. The match scores are turned into percentages that add up to one hundred.

c25.display: Fourth, blend. Each word carries a value, its useful meaning, and the asking word mixes in those values using the percentages. Query, key, value: that's the heart of attention.
c25.spoken: Fourth, blend. Each word carries a value, its useful meaning, and the asking word mixes in those values using the percentages. Query, key, value: that's the heart of attention.

c26.display: And the model doesn't do this just once. It has many attention heads, each looking at the same sentence in its own way.
c26.spoken: And the model doesn't do this just once. It has many attention heads, each looking at the same sentence in its own way.

c27.display: One head may follow grammar: who did what to whom.
c27.spoken: One head may follow grammar: who did what to whom.

c28.display: Another may link a word like it to the thing it refers to.
c28.spoken: Another may link a word like it to the thing it refers to.

c29.display: Another may simply watch the neighbouring words. Nobody assigns these jobs. They're learned during training, and many heads are hard to explain at all.
c29.spoken: Another may simply watch the neighbouring words. Nobody assigns these jobs. They're learned during training, and many heads are hard to explain at all.

c30.display: Put all of this together and you get a transformer: the design inside almost every modern chatbot. It's a stack of layers, and each layer does two things.
c30.spoken: Put all of this together and you get a transformer: the design inside almost every modern chatbot. It's a stack of layers, and each layer does two things.

c31.display: The vectors come in, fresh from Vector Valley.
c31.spoken: The vectors come in, fresh from Vector Valley.

c32.display: First, attention: the words look at each other and share meaning.
c32.spoken: First, attention: the words look at each other and share meaning.

c33.display: Then a feed-forward step, where each word thinks on its own for a moment, using what it just gathered.
c33.spoken: Then a feed-forward step, where each word thinks on its own for a moment, using what it just gathered.

c34.display: And then it repeats, layer after layer, dozens of times. With every layer, the understanding of the sentence gets a little deeper.
c34.spoken: And then it repeats, layer after layer, dozens of times. With every layer, the understanding of the sentence gets a little deeper.

c35.display: There is one limit. The model can only pay attention to what it can see. That's called the context window: the most tokens it can look at in one go, including your prompt, the chat so far, and its own answer.
c35.spoken: There is one limit. The model can only pay attention to what it can see. That's called the context window: the most tokens it can look at in one go, including your prompt, the chat so far, and its own answer.

c36.display: Early chatbots could hold a few thousand tokens. Many today can hold hundreds of thousands.
c36.spoken: Early chatbots could hold a few thousand tokens. Many today can hold hundreds of thousands.

c37.display: Think of a desk. Only what fits on the desk can be read at once. Anything that falls off the edge is simply not there.
c37.spoken: Think of a desk. Only what fits on the desk can be read at once. Anything that falls off the edge is simply not there.

c38.display: But even inside the window, attention isn't perfectly even. Researchers in 2023 hid a fact at different places in a long prompt, and asked models to find it.
c38.spoken: But even inside the window, attention isn't perfectly even. Researchers in 2023 hid a fact at different places in a long prompt, and asked models to find it.

c39.display: Facts near the start, and near the end, were found most often. Facts in the middle were missed more.
c39.spoken: Facts near the start, and near the end, were found most often. Facts in the middle were missed more.

c40.display: They called it "lost in the middle". Newer models are much better at this, but the habit is worth knowing about.
c40.spoken: They called it "lost in the middle". Newer models are much better at this, but the habit is worth knowing about.

c41.display: Time for "Try it yourself": a pause-and-guess quiz you can run on any chatbot.
c41.spoken: Time for "Try it yourself": a pause-and-guess quiz you can run on any chatbot.

c42.display: First, ask it: "I saw her duck. What does that mean?" Before it answers, make your own guess. Is it a bird, or someone bending down?
c42.spoken: First, ask it: "I saw her duck. What does that mean?" Before it answers, make your own guess. Is it a bird, or someone bending down?

c43.display: Then add a little context: "I saw her duck behind the wall." Ask again, and watch how a few extra words change the meaning it picks.
c43.spoken: Then add a little context: "I saw her duck behind the wall." Ask again, and watch how a few extra words change the meaning it picks.

c45.display: The myth: the model reads your prompt one word at a time, left to right, like we do.
c45.spoken: The myth: the model reads your prompt one word at a time, left to right, like we do.

c46.display: The reality: it reads the whole prompt at once, in parallel. Every word looks at every other word at the same time. Only the answer is written one token at a time, and that's our next stop.
c46.spoken: The reality: it reads the whole prompt at once, in parallel. Every word looks at every other word at the same time. Only the answer is written one token at a time, and that's our next stop.

c47.display: And here's your "Use it tomorrow" tip: put key instructions at the start or end of long prompts.
c47.spoken: And here's your "Use it tomorrow" tip: put key instructions at the start or end of long prompts.

c48.display: If you paste in a long document, put your main instruction first. For very long prompts, repeat it at the end. And keep the long reference text in the middle.
c48.spoken: If you paste in a long document, put your main instruction first. For very long prompts, repeat it at the end. And keep the long reference text in the middle.

c49.display: Let's stamp the passport. Attention lets every word look at every other word, and decide which ones matter.
c49.spoken: Let's stamp the passport. Attention lets every word look at every other word, and decide which ones matter.

c50.display: That's how bank finds river, and how it finds the animal. Stack attention into dozens of layers and you get a transformer, reading everything inside its context window at once.
c50.spoken: That's how bank finds river, and how it finds the animal. Stack attention into dozens of layers and you get a transformer, reading everything inside its context window at once.
